objective: Connect the Glasgow surname branches into one extended family tree, developing and testing tentative connections from the earliest records first.
common_origin: The owner reports that all men tested share the Glasgow Y-DNA lineage. A shared paternal origin around 1400–1450, possibly earlier, is the working research model; the founder, date and intervening generations remain to be identified.
later_records: Use records after 1850 when they can resolve an earlier identity, migration or branch connection; routine descendant reconstruction is secondary.

metrics.family_heads: Male surname bearers without a father in the selected pedigree and with at least two surname-bearing children; also queue heads with at least two descendants through one child.
metrics.components: Separate paternal components, including isolated surname bearers. Mothers, spouses and marriage connections cannot join surname branches.
metrics.largest_component: Percentage of the selected historical surname cohort in its largest paternal component.
metrics.confidence: Show confidently marked links and the working pedigree separately. Existing tree grades are not a claim that every underlying record has been independently audited.
metrics.baseline: Preserve the initial cohort IDs and input fingerprint. Compare the same surviving baseline people as well as current totals; report additions and missing people separately. Do not improve the score with a virtual founder, invented parent or incompatible alternative fathers.
metrics.target: One connected paternal component and 100% connected pairs in the working pedigree; a complete pedigree can retain one earliest family head. Keep the strongly assessed result separate.

early_connections.title: Glasgow burgess = Stirling John, provisionally
early_connections.status: Selected uncertain same-person identity; father–son alternative retained
early_connections.basis: Select the Glasgow burgess of 1447–1455 and the Stirling witness of 1475–1479/80 as the same man, at low confidence. Both groups use compatible John de Glasgu/Glasgw name forms in burgh-property witnessing, and the August 1475 catalogue places the Stirling John among burgesses. An adult active in 1447 could still witness in 1480 in his fifties or older. The conventional circa-1450 Stirling birth was inferred from an assumed young adult in 1475; it cannot establish a second man. A single compatible civic career is the simpler working model than inserting another generation from that estimate. No shared holding, relative, trade, personal seal or distinctive repeated associate joins the cities. The Glasgow-to-Stirling change is not itself evidence of migration. Father–son, other kin and two unrelated namesakes remain viable alternatives. The name may still be a personal byname; this selection does not prove hereditary surname transmission. The two Glasgow acts remain one high-confidence group and the three Stirling acts another; only their cross-group identity is selected uncertain. No birth, death or additional parent is inferred.
early_connections.next_test: Compare original Glasgow BL68/BL82 with Stirling B66/25/43 and Darow entries for unabridged names, title recitals and endorsements. Distinguish the charter parties’ seals from John’s own identification; no personal seal of Glesgw is established.
early_connections.metric_note: One documentary identity selected; no new paternal edge, profile denominator change or component-join credit. Named working ancestor reaches back to 1447.

early_connections.title: Stirling John → Saltmarket family
early_connections.status: Selected uncertain father; identity/degree alternatives retained
early_connections.basis: Select John Glasgw of Stirling as the uncertain father of Saltmarket John, using Glasgow-1095 as a provisional Saltmarket representative. Stirling John was an adult witness by 1475 and a burgess in the August charter description. That fits an older generation than the Saltmarket owner, securely recorded in 1527 and conditionally associated with the adult alias-Smith purchaser in 1506. The uncommon name, consecutive civic-property settings and the weak Brady/Brade surname-network clue support the existing leading father hypothesis. The Saltmarket parcel passing to William by 1528/29 favours placing this candidate with William’s family. The imported profile is a conflated placeholder whose biography also points to the Stirling witness. It is not proved to be Saltmarket John. If it instead represents the Stirling man, this proposed father link collapses as an identity duplicate. The 1506 alias-Smith identity and circa-1480 birth are conditional; no kinship clause or shared holding joins Stirling to Saltmarket. Brother, cousin, other predecessor or unrelated namesake remain alternatives. The later 15 October review selects the 1447–1455 Glasgow burgess and Stirling witness as one uncertain working identity. Father–son and other-family alternatives remain unselected; the two documentary groups stay separately inspectable.
early_connections.next_test: Follow title recitals and shared witnesses into the Saltmarket holding; compare the 1506 alias-Smith charter without equating its John to Saltmarket John in advance.
early_connections.metric_note: Together these two selected edges join one previously separate profile component; the named father is not added to the profile denominator.

early_connections.title: Place Alan in the earliest family
early_connections.status: Selected uncertain father; identity/degree alternatives retained
early_connections.basis: Select son, at low confidence, from the existing son/brother/nephew comparison with John Glasgw of Stirling. John’s adult activity in 1475–1480 is compatible with fathering a man killed before the 1494/95 proceeding. The rare surname in the same late-fifteenth-century record horizon makes this named household a useful provisional placement; no invented intermediary is needed. The father choice supplies a revisable one-generation model, rather than claiming that the court record names John. No age, home, occupation or relative is named for Alan. Brother, nephew or another early family remain viable, and the father choice is weaker than the Saltmarket hypothesis. Jedburgh is the court venue, not Alan’s residence or death place; Pilmure’s Ednem association and Ker’s surety do not supply Alan’s kin. The printed 1494/95 year and regnal-year discrepancy await manuscript collation. No mother, wife, child, exact birth or exact death is inferred.
early_connections.next_test: Inspect JC1/1 and the associated remission for Alan's kin or the parties owed satisfaction, then compare those names with the Stirling witnesses.

early_connections.title: Fisherrow household ↔ Corsankell through Edward

early_connections.basis: The visually checked printed index places Edward in Fischerraw at the same 8 July 1624 registration reference, 9/135, as James the tailor and his son Alexander. If Edward is Glasgow-1557, this associates Fisherrow with his tentative Corsankell line. The shared registration reference supports a concrete connection test, not a chosen brother, uncle or father relationship; Edward’s own father remains uncertain. Printed Indexes 44 pp.159–160 additionally associate Alexander with James, weaver, at 33/258, 33/360 and 34/287; Edward shares 33/258. This is a repeated property network, with the tailor/weaver identity unresolved. Eduard-994, indexed in 1609 with father James, is a compatible alternative for Edward. His identification could place the association within James-991’s proposed family; no new external branch connection is established.

early_connections.title: Agnes of Milneburne → James Glasgow younger
early_connections.status: Selected uncertain father; rival generations retained
early_connections.basis: Select James Glasgow younger (Glasgow-3921), the Corsankell tenant, as Agnes’s uncertain working father. Her probable 1601 and compatible 1606 Milneburne sasines and her 1628 Stevenston testament place her in the same small parish as the documented Corsankell family of 1559–1571. James younger’s approximate 1540 generation is a natural fit for the father of a woman already married by 1601. His existing plausible daughters Katherine Glasgow-1495 and Geillis Glasgow-3179 belong to the neighbouring Stevenston–Ardrossan women’s network; Geillis’s 1603 estate also names a James Glasgow in Stevenston in its debts. These are local family comparisons, not proved sisters or identification of the creditor. The earlier James-1168/Margaret Smith placement mixed two generations: Margaret is associated with the younger James, not the elder. Selecting the younger James gives the leading generational placement without inheriting that unsupported mother.
early_connections.next_test: Read the original 1601 and 1606 sasines and Agnes’s testament for named kin; compare the Logan and Corsankell households without assuming sisters or transferring Margaret as mother.

early_connections.title: Saltcoats sailor → Corsankell John, provisionally
early_connections.status: Selected uncertain father; grandson/collateral alternatives retained
early_connections.basis: Select John Glasgow-3193, the recorded son at Corsankell in 1571 and probable Kilwinning tenant of 1559–60, as the Saltcoats sailor John Glasgow-4152’s uncertain working father. Saltcoats in Ardrossan adjoins the Stevenston–Kilwinning coastal parish cluster where this earlier Glasgow family is documented. A later-sixteenth-century son of the earlier adult could have been a working sailor and father of two daughters by 1636. The choice gives the Saltcoats household a provisional place in an existing local John line, using geography and a feasible generation. It is a low-confidence selection, not a named parent clause or an identification of the two Johns. No source names the sailor’s parents or age. His former c.1600 birth was an unsupported creation estimate; it is not replaced by an invented older birth to fit this hypothesis. If a birth near 1600 is eventually established, the earlier John would have been an older father, and a grandson or more distant collateral placement could be more natural. Same given name is weak support and does not distinguish this candidate securely from Glasgow-3921 (James younger), another member of the local family, or an unrecorded father. The sailor could belong elsewhere in that family or to another branch. The 1559–60 Kilwinning attribution to the Corsankell John is itself probable, although the 1571 Corsankell family is directly recorded. The same-person alternative is less economical: an adult in 1559 would have been about 95 or older at the sailor’s death in 1636, assuming adulthood at eighteen. That is an illustrative age comparison, not a proved exclusion. The father-versus-grandfather degree remains open. No mother is assigned to the sailor or to his daughters; Agnes Wilson’s joint tenancy does not make her his mother, and Isobell Gray’s widowhood does not prove her maternity. The girls’ already-proved father links remain proved. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree save or confidence upgrade is made.
early_connections.next_test: A named parent, heir, maritime/property associate or succession record; establish the sailor’s age before choosing father versus grandfather with more confidence.

early_connections.title: Kilbirnie minister → John’s Kilwinning working family
early_connections.status: Selected uncertain father; previous father and duplicate retained
early_connections.basis: Select Glasgow-1604 as the uncertain working father of Rev. Glasgow-1073. The minister’s approximate 1653 birth fits an approximate 1626 father generation, and his Kilbirnie ministry and Robertland-Cunningham marriage belong to the Ayrshire setting of the Kilwinning profile. This adopts the leading existing-profile comparison already recorded in the research. Glasgow-1604’s attached adult sons have Kilwinning and Ayr households, making this a more economical local family placement than importing the minister into Glasgow-1078’s Glasgow-city household. No inspected record names the minister’s father; the preference rests on generation and locality, with low confidence. Glasgow-1604 is a tree-derived generation: his c.1626 birth, c.1664 death and parentage are unproved. The minister’s c.1653 birth is inferred from his reported age at death, not a baptism. Glasgow-3375, father with Barbara Alason in Kilwinning in 1679 and January 1689, remains a possible duplicate of the minister before his recorded January 1690 marriage. The two profile accounts are retained separately; their shared proposed father does not establish two distinct sons or brotherhood. No merge is selected. The former Glasgow-1078 father remains an uncertain, unselected alternative. The captured Cunningham-22604 mother is independently unproved; her tree attachment to Robert does not establish the minister’s maternity or make her Glasgow-1604’s wife. No new mother or spouse is assigned. The working route above Glasgow-1604 through Hugh Glasgow-1603 and James Glasgow-991 remains an unsupported older scaffold. The suggested Corsankell route is another unresolved ancestry comparison; this selection does not establish either path to the sixteenth-century family. The minister’s child-group audit remains open. Profile-based connectivity counts do not resolve duplicates or turn any uncertain link into documented descent. No new original inspection, confidence upgrade or live WikiTree edit is claimed.
early_connections.next_test: Identify a record naming the minister’s parent, and compare the 1679/1689 John–Barbara entries with his career. Establish the older Hugh generation separately.

early_connections.title: Jean, the 1654 Glen mother → John of Linlithgow
early_connections.status: Selected uncertain father through possible identity; no merge
early_connections.basis: Select John Glasgow-1561 as the uncertain working father of Jean Glasgow-3083, the mother named in the 1654 Issobell Glen baptism citation. The existing Linlithgow father study places an indexed daughter Jean in John’s household in 1613, represented by Glasgow-3055. The later mother’s profile also places her in Linlithgow. A child baptised in 1613 could have been a mother in 1654, about 41 years later if baptised in infancy. The 1626 birth stated for the later mother has no identified birth source and is not a concrete conflict with that identity. Prefer the possible same-woman explanation and carry the existing father comparison to the adult account, at low confidence. This is a selected inference from the existing local family and chronology, not a parent named in the 1654 citation. The profiles Glasgow-3055 and Glasgow-3083 remain separate accounts of a possible single woman. The selection establishes neither two distinct daughters called Jean nor a completed identity merge. The 1613 daughter’s later whereabouts are not established. Another Jean in another Glasgow household remains possible; a later daughter in John’s wider family is another explanation. The 1654 citation identifies Jean Glasgow as Issobell Glen’s mother, but its full event fields and original page have not been re-read here. Linlithgow for the adult account comes from her existing profile field, not a newly verified place clause in that baptism. Age 41 assumes baptism near birth and is an illustrative compatibility check, not a recorded maternal age. The 1626 profile year stays an unproved estimate; do not silently replace it with a proved 1613 birth. The saved accounts give 7 and 17 July 1613 and cite both X1RX-HPY and X1RX-HPB; retain these literal differences pending the original register. They are not counted as independent corroborating events. No mother, marriage date, husband’s given name or new child profile is inferred. John’s own selected Andrew-of-Calder father remains uncertain and is not proved by Andrew’s testament. No new original inspection, certain relationship upgrade, live WikiTree edit or identity merge is claimed. Connectivity continues to count profile accounts and therefore does not resolve this possible duplicate.
early_connections.next_test: Compare the literal 1613 baptism references and read the 1654 original for residence, spouse and witnesses; test the adult continuity without assuming a 1626 birth.
